summary: Nortriptyline is a secondary-amine tricyclic antidepressant used for depression and (off-label) neuropathic pain. It carries a boxed warning for increased suicidality in children, adolescents and young adults. Usual adult dose is 25 mg three to four times daily, up to 150 mg/day, with plasma monitoring (therapeutic window 50-150 ng/mL) above 100 mg/day. Anticholinergic effects and cardiotoxicity in overdose are key concerns.
indications: Relief of symptoms of depression (endogenous depression more likely to respond)

dosage.d: 25 mg three or four times daily; or total daily dose once daily
dosage.n: Start low and titrate; monitor plasma level if >100 mg/day

dosage.d: 30-50 mg/day in divided doses or once daily

dosage.n: Continue for adequate period after remission
Doses above 150 mg/day not recommended; keep plasma 50-150 ng/mL

admin: Administer orally as capsules; not recommended for children
Initiate at a low dose and increase gradually per clinical response and tolerance
Monitor plasma levels (optimum 50-150 ng/mL) when daily dose exceeds 100 mg
Allow at least 14 days between an MAOI and nortriptyline in either direction
Reduce dose for minor adverse effects; discontinue promptly for serious or allergic reactions
moa: The antidepressant mechanism is not fully established. Nortriptyline inhibits reuptake of norepinephrine (and to a lesser extent serotonin) at presynaptic neurons, increasing synaptic monoamine availability. It also antagonizes histamine, serotonin and acetylcholine receptors, accounting for sedative and anticholinergic effects, and interferes with catecholamine transport, release and storage.

absolute: Concomitant MAOIs or within 14 days (serotonin syndrome risk)
Concomitant linezolid or IV methylene blue
Hypersensitivity to nortriptyline or other tricyclics
Acute recovery period after myocardial infarction
monitor: Suicidality, especially early treatment and dose changes

preg: Limited human data. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Neonatal withdrawal/anticholinergic effects possible with third-trimester exposure.
lact: Nortriptyline is excreted in breast milk in small amounts. Exercise caution and weigh benefits against risks; monitor the infant for sedation and anticholinergic effects.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is provided; use with caution and monitor in renal impairment.
hepatic: Nortriptyline is extensively metabolized by the liver; use lower doses and monitor closely in hepatic impairment.

major: MAOIs (including linezolid, IV methylene blue) - hypertensive crisis / serotonin syndrome; contraindicated
Other serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol, triptans) - serotonin syndrome
Class IA/III antiarrhythmics and QT-prolonging drugs - additive cardiac conduction risk
CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine, quinidine, bupropion) - increased nortriptyline levels
moderate: CNS depressants and alcohol - additive sedation
Enzyme inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) - decreased levels
minor: Clonidine and guanethidine - reduced antihypertensive effect
Thyroid hormone - enhanced antidepressant and arrhythmic effects
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; it potentiates CNS and respiratory depression and increases overdose lethality.
interactions.diagnostics: Can alter ECG (QRS widening, QT prolongation); may cause false test results in some assays.

serious: Cardiac arrhythmias, heart block, QT prolongation
emergency: Severe arrhythmia or cardiac arrest (especially overdose)

monitoring: Mood, suicidality and behavioral changes, especially in first weeks and at dose changes
Baseline and periodic ECG, particularly in older patients or cardiac disease
Plasma nortriptyline level (50-150 ng/mL) when dose exceeds 100 mg/day
Blood pressure (orthostatic), CBC if signs of dyscrasia
counsel: Watch for and report worsening mood, agitation or thoughts of self-harm, especially early in treatment
May take 2-4 weeks for full antidepressant effect; do not stop abruptly
Rise slowly to avoid dizziness; expect dry mouth and constipation
Avoid alcohol and other sedatives; use caution driving until effects known
Use sunscreen due to photosensitivity; tell prescriber of all medicines (MAOIs contraindicated)
pearls: BOXED WARNING: increased suicidality in children, adolescents and young adults (<=24 years) - monitor closely; not approved in pediatrics
Therapeutic plasma window 50-150 ng/mL; both low and high levels reduce efficacy
Secondary amine - fewer anticholinergic/sedative effects than amitriptyline
Highly cardiotoxic in overdose (QRS widening predicts toxicity) - prescribe limited quantities to at-risk patients
Contraindicated within 14 days of an MAOI
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered unless it is almost time for the next dose; then skip it. Do not double the dose. For once-daily bedtime dosing, skip a missed dose if it is morning to avoid daytime drowsiness.
overdose: TCA overdose can be fatal. Critical features include cardiac dysrhythmias, QRS widening, severe hypotension, seizures and CNS depression/coma. Obtain ECG and begin continuous cardiac monitoring immediately, secure the airway, IV access and gastric decontamination; sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening/arrhythmia. Contact a poison control center; observe at least 6 hours with cardiac monitoring.
